Special Commission of Inquiry
into Healthcare Funding
Before: The Commissioner,
Mr Richard Beasley SC
At Level 2, 121 Macquarie Street,
Sydney, New South Wales
Tuesday, 19 November 2024 at 10.00am
(Day 062)
Mr Ed Muston SC (Senior Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ross Glover (Counsel Assisting)
Dr Tamsin Waterhouse (Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ian Fraser (Counsel Assisting)
Mr Daniel Fuller (Counsel Assisting)
Also present:
Mr Hilbert Chiu SC with Ms Joanna Davidson for NSW Health

THE COMMISSIONER: Good morning, Mr Muston.
MR MUSTON: Good morning. We've got a large panel of --
THE COMMISSIONER: I can see.
MR MUSTON: -- chief executives or predominantly chief
executives this morning. Sitting I think from your left to
right is Jude Constable, the acting chief executive of
Central Coast LHD; Margot Mains, the chief executive of
Illawarra Shoalhaven LHD; Peter Collins, the board chair of
Nepean Blue Mountains LHD; Lee Gregory, the acting chief
executive of Nepean Blue Mountains LHD; Tobi Wilson, the
chief executive of South East Sydney LHD; Dominic Morgan,
the chief executive of New South Wales Ambulance - did look
up to make sure that my list matches up with who's there -
Cathryn Cox, the chief executive of the Sydney Children's
Hospitals Network; and Wendy Hoey, the acting chief
executive of Justice Health.
THE COMMISSIONER: Any more and we would run out of room,
I think.
MR MUSTON: That's true.
THE COMMISSIONER: So, yes, good luck.
MR MUSTON: And I have a list that tells me that Jude
Constable, Dominic Morgan, Cathryn Cox and Wendy Hoey will
take an affirmation and the balance will take an oath.
<JUDE CONSTABLE, affirmed [10.01 am]
<DOMINIC MORGAN, affirmed
<CATHRYN COX, affirmed
<WENDY HOEY, affirmed
<MARGOT MAINS, sworn
<PETER COLLINS, sworn

<TOBI WILSON, sworn

<EXAMINATION BY MR MUSTON:
THE COMMISSIONER: I think we know who everyone is. Do
you need to go through --
MR MUSTON: The only reason I was going to ask each of
them to give us their name is for the benefit of the people
who are transcribing it today, who are offsite, just to
make sure that they know who's --
THE COMMISSIONER: All right. As usual, it's better
I don't interfere. So you go ahead and do it your way.
MR MUSTON: I was going to do it in a short-circuited way.
Could I ask each of you, going along the table, just to
state your name for the record so the people who are
transcribing this remotely today can recognise your voice
and make sure they know who's talking when you're speaking.
MS CONSTABLE: Jude Constable.
MS MAINS: Margot Mains.
MR COLLINS: Peter Collins,
MR GREGORY: Lee Gregory.
MR WILSON: Tobi Wilson.
DR MORGAN: Dominic Morgan.
MS COX: Cathryn Cox.
MS HOEY: Wendy Hoey.
MR MUSTON: Can I quickly start with you, Wendy. A number
of you have prepared statements, which have been tendered
previously in the Inquiry, and you've each adopted them.
Wendy, I think - I should say Ms Hoey, you've prepared a --
THE COMMISSIONER: One more "Wendy" and I was going to say
something.
MR MUSTON: We're very relaxed and friendly down here.
It's an exchange of ideas. You've prepared a statement
dated 13 November 2024 to assist the Inquiry. It's your

most recent statement; is that correct?
MS HOEY: Yes.
MR MUSTON: Have you had an opportunity to review that
this morning before giving your evidence?
MS HOEY: Yes.
MR MUSTON: You're satisfied that its contents are to the
best of your knowledge true and correct?
MS HOEY: I have one change, which I think we probably
informed you of.
MR MUSTON: Yes, sorry. I also have that. That is
paragraph 55?
MS HOEY: Yes. Yes.
MR MUSTON: Just tell us what the correction that you wish
to make to paragraph 55 is.
MS HOEY: Where it says that the delivered cost saving has
been delivered primarily to Justice Health New South Wales,
that's actually to the justice sector.
THE COMMISSIONER: Sorry, I've just missed that. What
line are we looking at?
MS HOEY: It's on page 13 of - paragraph 55, just at the
end there, Commissioner.
THE COMMISSIONER: Right. Okay. Thank you.
MR MUSTON: I might start, Ms Hoey, just by asking you
some questions about Justice Health.
MS HOEY: Sure.
MR MUSTON: Could you, just in broad outline, explain to
us the services that are provided by Justice Health to the
New South Wales prison population?
MS HOEY: Yes. So we're Justice Health and Forensic
Mental Health Network, and we've got sort of two arms of
our services. So there's the forensic mental health

system, which we'll park just now and think about the
custodial system. So there's over a hundred locations but
37 I think just now custodial centres and seven youth
justice centres, and we provide primary care, mental health
care, population health and public health, drug and alcohol
services, and a range of other primary care services to the
inmates across New South Wales.
MR MUSTON: And I think you tell us in your statement that
adds up to approximately 13,000 patients?
MS HOEY: Yes, the population of adult centres is roughly
about - sits around 13,000 - it can go up and down by a
thousand or two every so often - and I think just now
there's about 220 in youth detention centres.
MR MUSTON: So that's the prison population. What about
forensic mental health?
MS HOEY: Yes. The forensic mental health, so that prison
population we would also do custodial mental health to
there, which is almost like a general mental health service
within a forensic setting. Then we have - within our
control in our budget is a 135-bed high secure forensic
hospital at Malabar and also our primary care - our primary
court diversion centre - service both for adults and for
youth, also our community forensic mental health service,
which provides advice, risk assessment to all the LHDs
across New South Wales, and also have a sort of
relationship responsibility to all the medium secures and
low secures across the state and also all the forensic
patients that are within LHDs, which - where the majority
of forensic mental health patients are.
MR MUSTON: In terms of the forensic patients, when we had
our trip out to the forensic hospital you were describing
to us issues of bed block which affect the forensic
hospital in much the same way as they affect - or we've
been told they affect hospitals around the state. Could
you just explain to us the way in which bed block operates
in the context of the forensic hospital?
MS HOEY: So if somebody comes before the court and is
given defence under the Mental Health and Cognitive
Impairment Forensic Provisions Act, so they would be
detained in - or the MHRT, the Mental Health Review
Tribunal, would detain them, so that could be to a forensic

mental health high secure hospital, medium secure, low
secure. They can also detain within the prison setting as
well, and unfortunately we have 27 forensic patients in our
prison setting just now awaiting health beds, not under a
custodial order but under a health order, and that's
because within our high secure forensic mental health
setting we have patients waiting for medium secure, and as
well in medium secure, which is from where the LHDs, they
have patients awaiting to get out and to do that
rehabilitation. So they're just general bed block across
the system.
MR MUSTON: So in a practical sense that means if you're
not able to move patients through the high secure setting
when they are theoretically ready to be transitioned into a
medium secure and then to a lower secure setting from
within the forensic hospital, bed block means a mental
health patient or a patient who enters the justice system
through the mental health track will end up in a prison
setting unless and until such time as a vacancy becomes
available or a bed becomes available in a mental health
hospital?
MS HOEY: Correct. And, if you look at our sort of policy
of least restriction, it's hard to uphold that when people
are being held in prison when they should be in high
secure, and in high secure when they should be in medium
through. So falling through.
MR MUSTON: It would seem logical - and perhaps it's more
a question for your psychiatrist colleagues, but the
consequences in terms of the progress of one's mental
illness of being sent into a prison rather than placed into
a mental health facility would seem to be negative; would
that be a fair assumption?
MS HOEY: Yes, I think we would all agree that the best
place to be cared for for a health presentation or for
health rehabilitation is in a health environment.
MR MUSTON: What are some of the challenges that you face
in transitioning patients out of that high secure mental
health setting into a medium secure setting at a time when
they are perhaps ready to move medically?
MS HOEY: I think generally there's lack of beds and bed
movement, but also moving from a high secure to a medium

secure, these patients that we're managing have got quite
high risk factors and that's always - you know, moving them
down to a lower acuity is a big decision to make, and
sometimes if there's not the resources to be able to
adequately manage that risk or the perceived risk that
people are presenting it can be difficult to get them
through. It's also the fact that we have civil patients
who have, you know, been very difficult to manage and
they've sometimes harmed people within general mental
health services that we would take into our high secure,
and stepping those people back down into the environments
is hard because people are often - they've had really bad
experiences or people have been hurt and that makes it even
more challenging, I think.
MR MUSTON: Stepping them transitionally through high
security to medium security within the setting of the
forensic hospital is something presumably you're able to do
as soon as you're able to move people out at the bottom, as
it were?
MS HOEY: Yes.
MR MUSTON: And what about moving patients from a forensic
hospital into forensic settings or mental health settings
within the LHDs? Where that's possible, how does that
work?
MS HOEY: All the medium secures are run by the LHDs. So
if we are moving anybody out of our high secure hospital
they're always going into an LHD environment, so they're
going out with our clinical governance into an LHD's unit.
So it's a change of treating team, change of psychiatry
going through there.
MR MUSTON: Are there any particular barriers that you
have experienced in transitioning patients from the high
secure setting at the forensic hospital out into wards
within the LHDs?
MS HOEY: We would generally from high secure go into a
medium secure. We wouldn't generally be moving from -
apart from our civil patients, from a high secure into a
general ward within an LHD. But it's the same, I think,
it's access to beds, access to expertise, and the risk that
sometimes our patients carry can be quite daunting.

MR MUSTON: You said that the medium secure facilities are
run by the LHDs.
MS HOEY: Yes.
MR MUSTON: Do you think there might be some advantage to
Justice Health, albeit in a different setting, having
perhaps a greater involvement in the operation of medium
secure facilities across the state?
MS HOEY: Yes, we have developed a new forensic mental
health strategy and policy, which gives a little bit more
strength to our New South Wales clinical director for
forensic psychiatry, and also through the SWMHIP program.
So there's been investment in builds. We have been -
Justice Health has been given beds within that. So we'll
be trialing that soon to see if it does help for Justice
Health to have that governance over the patient journey, if
you like, and I suppose be the ones to make the decisions
about where people are going after the forensic hospital.
MR MUSTON: So, in addition to the decision-making power
potentially resting with Justice Health, there's also
presumably going to be a funding consequence. Would it be
right that under that arrangement the staffing of those
facilities would come out of Justice Health's budget rather
than out of the budget of the LHDs?
MS HOEY: Yes. So the unit that we've been allocated
through the SWMHIP program, we'll have the operational
budget for that when it comes, when it's built, and we get
the operational budget for that. Yes, that will come into
Justice Health's control.
MR MUSTON: You mentioned a moment ago diversion programs
that are run by Justice Health. Could you just explain to
us what those programs are in a nutshell?
MS HOEY: Yes. So we have adult and youth, so - diversion
programs, which is we work within the local courts where
people who have non-indictable offences we can divert to
mental health services, and with the adults we've been
lucky enough to secure funding and we're rolling out over a
three-year program to be in every court in New South Wales,
and we're getting some really, really good outcomes from
that, particularly in the regional areas, where there's a
high level of Aboriginal diversions occurring. And then

with the youth courts, unfortunately we're only in
10 per cent of the youth courts, but the courts that we are
in we've got really good outcomes with diverting kids from
the criminal justice system into mental health care.
MR MUSTON: When you say "good outcomes", obviously
transferring someone who's got a mental health problem into
a mental health setting is probably a good outcome in and
of itself. But, in terms of broader outcomes of that, do
you have any measured outcomes in terms of recidivism and a
re-presentation within the justice system?
MS HOEY: Yes, we do. I don't have the figures for
recidivism here, but there's been a number of research
papers published around the efficacy of the adult - more
than the kids - the adult program. But I think probably
one of our better pieces of work was the cost-benefit
analysis around adult court diversion, where I think it was
every dollar spent we get $4 back to the government around
the reducing of custodial. I mean, anybody going into
custody or into the criminal justice system, it's
criminogenic in itself and certainly is not helpful from a
health perspective. So reducing the costs for custodial
care, reducing the costs to society longer term, reducing
recidivism, so reducing crime. So I think we do a good
job, and the benefit's across government, it's not all to
health, and then obviously there's a longer term reduction
to the health burden as we get them into health care
earlier and all their associated comorbidities as well as
mental health associated with that.
MR MUSTON: So the diversion program not only potentially
diverts individuals on a longer term out of the criminal
justice system but also perhaps provides an interventional
opportunity to deal with some of the social determinants of
health which might be sending them down a spiral?
MS HOEY: Definitely. Yes. We know that the social
determinants of justice are the same as the social
determinants of health. So if we can address them then
there's a double win, I suppose, yes.
MR MUSTON: Whilst you don't have the figures at a
headline level, I gather from what you've told us of levels
recidivism and the like, when assessed against those who
have not been through programs like this are much --

MS HOEY: Much lower, much lower, yes. And I think - it's
in my statement - there has been some Australian work done
and published around the savings that could be achieved
with more youth diversion, and I think it's in the level of
billions from an Australian perspective. We've not
necessarily done it specifically in New South Wales, but
certainly from an Australian perspective.
MR MUSTON: In terms of the - you mentioned a moment ago
the ability to intervene in people's health at a time when
they're either diverted through the mental health system
or, alternatively, when they are incarcerated. What are
the potential benefits as you see it of intervening from a
health perspective in these people's lives?
MS HOEY: Yes, often by the time somebody gets to us
there's been a lot of - there's been a lot of trauma in
their life, and if you look at what drives - what drives
somebody into custody is often, you know, out-of-home care,
housing, education. From a health perspective, we know
that people coming into prison have had less health
interventions, so general practitioner intervention, dental
intervention. So there's much higher rates of chronic
disease, there's much higher rates of drug and alcohol. So
anything that we --
THE COMMISSIONER: I'm pretty sure I was told when we
visited out to Malabar that 20 per cent of the prison
population have what could be described as complex mental
health issues.
MS HOEY: Yes.
THE COMMISSIONER: And it's often those - I was told those
mental health issues is what is causing them to end up in
prison in the first place; correct?
MS HOEY: Definitely as well, yes, yes.
THE COMMISSIONER: And what stuck in my mind is - I've
forgotten who it was, but being told that prisons are
becoming like asylums because it's the mental health issue
that's driving many people to committing crimes, they end
up in prison and then we don't have the resourcing to
properly treat the condition that is actually causing them
to offend and in many cases re-offend. Is that your memory
of what I was told?

MS HOEY: That would be a really good summary of the
psychiatrist's conversations with you, and I would agree
with that. The demand for mental health care in prisons is
relentless.
MR MUSTON: In terms of the mental health care and the
demand for mental health care in prisons you have told us
in paragraph 21 of your statement about the divide between
psychiatric care on the one hand and psychological care on
the other. I just wonder if you could explain how that
actually operates and what you see the consequences of that
as being for the prison population and the health outcomes
for the prison population?
MS HOEY: Yes, it's a very strange split in the way things
are managed, and I just know that ourselves and Corrective
Services and Youth Justice are trying to work through this
as best we can, but it is a tension point between our
services where Justice Health has predominantly been funded
for psychiatry and for nursing, and that's about
prescribing and providing medication, and Corrective
Services are funded for psychology, so psychological
interventions across mental health and drug and alcohol,
and behavioural management, and there's a little bit of a
tension point there because Corrective Services provides
psychological services within our criminogenic framework.
So they commence that at sentencing. So then you've got
all your remand folks who come in and out, and there's
quite a trend of coming in and out at the remand stage, who
don't necessarily get that psychological intervention from
a health perspective that we feel could really be
beneficial for them.
MR MUSTON: So, just unpacking that, the concept of
psychological care being delivered through a criminogenic
lens, that is psychologists who are retained principally
through Justice to try and prevent people from committing a
crime when they leave?
MS HOEY: Correct, yes, yes.
MR MUSTON: As opposed to - and not suggesting that there
may not be some overlap, but as opposed to providing
psychological care with the objective of treating the
mental illness - a mental illness that a patient might
have?

MS HOEY: Yes, or dealing with holistically that person's
psychological presentation or trauma. And it's not to say
that Corrective Services psychologists don't do mental
health. They do, but it's just from a different lens, and
I think particularly in the remand environment, where
people are going back out into health services, that that
continuity of care would be better if it's provided by
Health.
MR MUSTON: And so the consequence of the timing of the
delivery of this psychological care means people who are in
remand sometimes potentially for quite a lengthy period of
time awaiting sentence will not receive psychological care
within a prison setting?
MS HOEY: Correct, yes. They do certainly for behavioural
disturbance where it's a security issue within the prison.
MR MUSTON: So to the extent that a prisoner might be
demonstrating some behaviour - a prisoner on remand might
be demonstrating some behavioural problems --
MS HOEY: Yes.
MR MUSTON: -- which are posing a threat to other prisoners
or --
MS HOEY: Or themselves.
MR MUSTON: -- making it difficult to deal with them --
MS HOEY: Or themselves.
MR MUSTON: -- they might receive some psychological care?
MS HOEY: Yes, yes.
MR MUSTON: Is there any interface between the psychiatric
care that's delivered through Justice Health on the one
hand and the psychological care, that is to say are there
multidisciplinary team meetings and the like that happen
between the psychologists or the psychiatrists with respect
to the care of a particular patient?
MS HOEY: Yes, definitely. We do have MDTs, and the
psychology and the officers and everybody's involved in

that as much as we can. However, there is always a barrier
around the sharing of health information across the divide
of Health and Corrections or Health and Justice, and that's
really the medical legal and the responsibility of Health
to keep that information private and for what it's been
provided for, which is for health purposes, and the role of
the reporter as a psychologist working for Corrections and
the treatment - therapeutic treatment from Health. So
there's always - there's always been issues. We're trying
to work through it as best we can. We definitely share
risk and we do share patients and we do share treatment
plans, particularly for those most disturbed within the
system.
MR MUSTON: But just to unpack that a little bit in terms
of the information barrier, information which is provided
to psychologists in the context of a program delivered for
criminogenic purposes is available for use in decision
making around the way in which a prisoner might be - or an
inmate might be moved from one prison to another,
classified as high risk or low risk --
MS HOEY: Yes, self-placement, yes, yes.
MR MUSTON: Whereas information provided to medical
professionals who deliver care through Justice Health is
subject to the usual doctor/patient or clinician/patient
confidentiality such that --
MS HOEY: Yes, yes, but we do have - I mean, we've got
processes in place, a Health notification where we can tell
Corrective Services what we think needs to be done from a
risk mitigation perspective around self-placement or
medical holds perhaps to a metropolitan area if we believe
they need to be nearer one of the tertiary hospitals that
we share with.
MR MUSTON: Does the fact that information provided to
psychologists who are delivering these criminogenic
programs is able to be used for that wider range of
purposes compromise the extent to which those programs can
deliver good psychological care from a mental health point
of view rather than a purely criminogenic point of view, do
you think?
MS HOEY: They're different - you know, they're different
aims and so - I mean, Corrective Services - I don't want to

comment on their program, but they value what they're
doing, and from their perspective whether they're working
or not they can comment on. I'm not going to comment on
that. It's about recidivism. But certainly we have
evidence-based health programs that we believe would be
helpful.
MR MUSTON: In addition to the mental health work there's
obviously a range, as you've told us, of other primary care
which is delivered to inmates within the prison system?
MS HOEY: Yes.
MR MUSTON: That includes in a number of cases providing
anti-psychotic medication and the like to prisoners?
MS HOEY: For mental health, yes. Yes.
MR MUSTON: Which results in a large number of prisoners
or a larger number of prisoners perhaps than in the wider
society suffering from metabolic disease?
MS HOEY: Yes, we know that mental health in its own but
also combined with medication there's an increased risk of
metabolic disorder, so, you know, obesity and diabetes,
everything that goes with it.
THE COMMISSIONER: My note was - which I want to
check - is 95 per cent of the prison population have
metabolic disorder or disease; is that --
MS HOEY: Ninety-five per cent probably of mental health,
I would think, yes.
MR MUSTON: Meaning that a large proportion of the prison
population suffers from metabolic disease of some type?
MS HOEY: Yes, yes, and a high level of chronic disease
particularly within the Aboriginal cohorts that we manage,
which is 32 per cent of prison.
MR MUSTON: In terms of metabolic disease and other
co-morbidities, it's not just the delivery of primary
health care which is important in terms of trying to keep
these patients well and reducing long term their morbidity?
MS HOEY: Correct, yes.

MR MUSTON: Also --
MS HOEY: Prevention, health - health literacy, prevention
and health promotion.
MR MUSTON: Diet?
MS HOEY: Yes, diet definitely. We saw examples of that
in Long Bay.
MR MUSTON: That's what I was going to ask you about. In
essence you have a captive audience when it comes to the
delivery of a good diet. Is that something which Justice
Health is involved in from a dietetics point of view, or is
it something that's dealt with by Justice?
MS HOEY: Yes, it's got to be dealt with by both of us
because Corrections provide the food, or Justice provides
the food. We're providing the advice, if you like. So we
have developed our health --
THE COMMISSIONER: Your advice, I assume, doesn't extend
to "it's a good idea to give the prisoners a loaf of white
bread before they are locked down for the night"?
MS HOEY: No, that's not actually our advice. But we are
working together with them to try and change some of the
habits that are happening through our healthy prisons
framework. So we're starting with what we would call
buy-up, so that's the prison shop, if you like, and at
least having healthy alternatives available.
THE COMMISSIONER: Your organisation is responsible for
the health of the prison population, and did you say
13,000? You did?
MS HOEY: Yes.
THE COMMISSIONER: And not many of those people are what
are called lifers?
MS HOEY: No.
THE COMMISSIONER: Some will die in prison simply because
they might have committed a crime 30 years ago and they --

MS HOEY: Correct. The majority of people come --
THE COMMISSIONER: If you get a 20-year sentence when
you're in your 70s, you're probably not leaving prison.
But most people are getting out; correct?
MS HOEY: Correct, yes.
THE COMMISSIONER: And as a matter of logic when people
are released from prison it would be better if, as far as
possible, their mental health conditions have been
addressed and they're healthy?
MS HOEY: Correct.
THE COMMISSIONER: Because it would be better if they're
not becoming a burden on the public hospitals, is one
thing?
MS HOEY: That's correct.
THE COMMISSIONER: And it would be better if they had the
best possible chance to become economically active,
productive members of society?
MS HOEY: Correct.
THE COMMISSIONER: So if you're in charge of health why
wouldn't you be in charge of diet, given it's so related to
health? Why is Corrections in charge of diet?
MS HOEY: I think we provide health care.
THE COMMISSIONER: Yes.
MS HOEY: To the prison population.
THE COMMISSIONER: Yes.
MS HOEY: Corrections have the broader responsibility to
provide a roof over their head, a safe environment.
THE COMMISSIONER: Yes.
MS HOEY: Their food. So it's with Corrections.
THE COMMISSIONER: Does food make sense, though?

MS HOEY: Yes, because Corrective Services --
THE COMMISSIONER: It depends what it is, I suppose,
doesn't it?
MS HOEY: Yes. Yes, that's right, Corrective Services.
I think we have a responsibility from a health perspective
to work with Corrections to ensure that we're advising and
promoting healthy environments, and that's what we're
doing. I mean, they're linking in well --
THE COMMISSIONER: Would your advice in relation to the
diet that prisoners have be different to the diet that's
actually provided to them?
MS HOEY: Yes. Yes.
THE COMMISSIONER: In the sense that it would be --
MS HOEY: Wouldn't be white bread.
THE COMMISSIONER: It would be a healthier diet?
MS HOEY: Definitely a healthier diet.
THE COMMISSIONER: In the way we understood a good,
healthy --
MS HOEY: Correct.
THE COMMISSIONER: -- balanced diet to maintain a good
levels of weight instead of obesity?
MS HOEY: Yes, and exercise as well. You know, the
fundamentals of good health is what we'd be trying to push
through our healthy prisons framework.
MR MUSTON: You tell us in your statement of the
proportion of inmates who are First Nations people and you
mentioned it a moment ago. From that truly bleak statistic
on one view there emerges an opportunity to do some
potentially valuable work when it comes to closing the gap
in --
MS HOEY: Yes, I think fundamentally we have to say that
people in prison and the overrepresentation of Aboriginal

people is something that we need to address as a state and
as a country, and it's increasing. I think the fact that
people are in prison is an opportunity to intervene, but
shouldn't be the opportunity to intervene, and I think,
conversely, prison is not a healthy environment, so
although as the Commissioner's pointed out with the food
that's provided and exercise and the impacts on mental
health - so, while we're trying to improve somebody's
mental health, prison impacts on somebody's mental health,
and while we're trying to improve health literacy for
people then the opportunities to practise that health
literacy and practise that empowerment with the prisoners
is not there. So it's sort of a double-edged sword. But,
yes, we do want to be able to intervene as much as we can
while somebody's in prison, although I'd prefer to be doing
it in the community for them.
MR MUSTON: Which brings me to my next question. When one
looks to the statistics that you give us in relation to the
percentage of the youth prison population who are First
Nations people, that is even bleaker. That, on one view,
points to a real potential value in accelerating these
diversion programs within the youth setting that you've
mentioned?
MS HOEY: Yes, definitely. I think the diversion - and
we've seen by the experience of the expansion of the adult
into regional areas, so we've increased the number of
Aboriginal people who have been diverted because there's a
higher percentage in the regions, and within the children's
courts the regions were not in yet. So extending out to
those regional environments I think would be really good.
The thing with the youth is that they cycle through very,
